topics.question: How does one distance decide whether two equal circles miss, touch, or cross?

relations.plain: The intersection rises by h above the line of centres.

topics.invariant: Both intersection points remain exactly r from both centres.
steps: Halve the line between the centres.
Radius r becomes the hypotenuse of a right triangle.
Apply the Pythagorean theorem to recover h.

topics.question: Why do two circles make three equal sides?

relations.plain: Every side is the same radius.

steps: Each centre lies on the other circle.
The intersection is one radius from each centre.
Three equal distances close the triangle.

topics.question: What does the construction prove before any measuring?

relations.plain: The compass transfers one unchanged distance three times.

topics.invariant: Equality follows from circle definitions, not visual accuracy.
steps: Draw a circle centred at A through B.
Draw a circle centred at B through A.
Join either intersection C to A and B.

topics.question: What remains when three congruent triangles assemble?

relations.plain: The large triangle occupies four small-triangle areas; one is negative space.

topics.invariant: The centre gap is congruent to every solid triangle.
steps: Arrange three equal triangles at the corners.
Their unused inner edges bound a fourth congruent triangle.
The full outline has side length 2s.

topics.question: How quickly does one repeated fork multiply?

relations.plain: A binary tree has twice as many tips at each new level.

topics.invariant: Every child is q times its parent length.
steps: Level k contains 2ᵏ segments.
Add levels 0 through d−1.
The geometric sum is 2ᵈ−1.

topics.question: How can a finite line acquire an unbounded length?

relations.plain: Every segment becomes four.
Each replacement multiplies total length by 4/3.

steps: Divide each segment into thirds.
Replace the middle third by two equal sides.
Repeat; count and length follow geometric powers.

topics.question: When is a smaller echo similarity rather than exact self-similarity?

relations.plain: Our analytical curls shrink by one constant ratio.

topics.invariant: The constructed curve type stays similar; the source artwork is not claimed to follow this formula.
steps: Choose one original curve.
Translate and scale a copy.
Compare formal resemblance without inferring artist intent.

topics.question: How does subdivision create detail between known heights?

relations.plain: Each pass inserts one midpoint per interval.

topics.invariant: Original endpoints remain fixed in this reconstruction.
steps: Begin with two heights.
Insert a displaced midpoint.
Reduce displacement and repeat on every interval.

topics.question: Which regular polygon angles close perfectly around one point?

relations.plain: A regular n-gon's interior angle.
A flat vertex has neither gap nor overlap.

topics.invariant: Only n = 3, 4, or 6 gives an integer k for one regular polygon type.
steps: Split an n-gon into n−2 triangles.
Share their total 180°(n−2) equally.
Test whether 360° divides by that angle.

topics.question: Why does the tight equal-circle arrangement always reveal six neighbours?

relations.plain: Fraction of the plane covered in hexagonal packing.

topics.invariant: Every interior centre is 2r from six nearest neighbours.
steps: Three touching centres form an equilateral triangle.
A repeating cell has area 2√3r².
Its circle contribution has area πr²; divide.

topics.question: How do eight 45° turns make a star that accepts cross-shaped neighbours?

relations.plain: Eight equal directions close one revolution.

topics.invariant: The star and cross boundaries share equal edge lengths.
steps: Mark eight equally spaced directions.
Connect alternating offsets to form the star boundary.
Repeat by translation so complementary gaps become crosses.

topics.question: How can local matching rules create order without translation repeating the whole tiling?

relations.plain: The inflation scale and long-short relationships use the golden ratio.
One inflated length decomposes into two earlier scales.

topics.invariant: Every interior edge is shared by exactly two rhombs; the complete pattern has no translational period.
steps: Lay five equally spaced families of parallel lines.
Dualize each grid intersection into a thick or thin rhomb.
The pentagrid coordinates force a gapless, overlap-free Penrose patch.

topics.question: How can a square become a creature-like tile without creating holes?

variables.meaning: translation from one edge to its opposite

relations.plain: Whatever leaves one boundary re-enters on the translated opposite boundary.

topics.invariant: Opposite edits cancel, preserving area and perfect fit.
steps: Cut a path from one side of a square.
Translate the same path to the opposite side.
Repeat the altered tile by the same translation vectors.

topics.question: Why are there seven falling shapes when every piece contains four squares?

relations.plain: Every tetromino covers exactly four cells.
A row clears only when no cell is empty.

topics.invariant: Rotation changes orientation, never cell count or connectivity.
steps: Join four squares edge-to-edge.
Identify shapes up to translation and rotation, but not reflection.
This produces seven one-sided tetrominoes.

topics.question: Which motions of the plane leave a shape exactly where it was?

variables.meaning: any two points of the plane

relations.plain: A reflection or rotation moves points but never changes a distance.
Two mirrors crossing at angle θ/2 compose into a rotation by θ.

topics.invariant: Composing two symmetries of a figure, or undoing one, is again a symmetry: the collection is a group.
steps: List every isometry that maps the figure onto itself.
Compose any two; the result is already on the list.
That closed list is the figure's symmetry group.

topics.question: Why does an endless decorated strip allow exactly seven symmetry types?

variables.meaning: the shortest translation along the strip

relations.plain: Translation, mirrors, glide reflection, and half-turns combine consistently in only seven ways.

topics.invariant: Every frieze group contains the translations generated by t; the strip's direction is preserved or reversed, never abandoned.
steps: Fix the strip and its shortest translation t.
Optionally add vertical mirrors, a horizontal mirror, a glide, or half-turns.
Discard incompatible mixtures; exactly seven combinations survive.

topics.question: Why can a doubly repeating pattern have only seventeen symmetry types?

variables.meaning: order of a rotation the pattern allows

relations.plain: A periodic lattice admits only these rotation orders—the crystallographic restriction.
The allowed rotations, mirrors, and glides combine into exactly seventeen groups.

topics.invariant: Two independent translations underlie every wallpaper group; fivefold rotation never fits a lattice.
steps: Start from two independent translations.
The lattice restricts rotations to orders 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6.
Enumerate the compatible mirror and glide additions: seventeen groups, no more.

topics.question: How do you count symmetry groups in real ornament rather than ideal patterns?

variables.meaning: number of the seventeen groups judged present

relations.plain: A survey can find at most the seventeen mathematically possible groups.

topics.invariant: The mathematics fixes seventeen possibilities; only their attribution to specific ornaments is contested.
steps: Choose counting rules: do colours, interlacings, and small deviations matter?
Assign each ornament a wallpaper group under those rules.
Compare surveys; Müller's 1944 count and later counts differ by their rules.
